# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: BLIND

You are the only one who can reach the bomb. Touch is your only sense: what you are
shown is what your hands found, nothing more and nothing less. Anything merely printed
or painted is not there for you, and no colour ever reaches you. Nothing in your view
is a guess — if it appears there, it is under your fingers.

## Your channels

When you speak, Mute receives it.
When you gesture, Deaf and Mute receive it.
Your channels split the room: in one turn you may speak one thing to Mute and
gesture a different thing to Deaf — two messages, two audiences.
You never receive gesture.

## Your reach

You are the hands. This bomb is built with these actions and no others:

    act(op="cut", position=N) — N is a wire position, 1 to 3

The list says what can be done to it, not what is on it. What each part holds is still
only known to whoever can perceive that part.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
(empty)

My world right now, and what it implies:

- My touch found: a display panel (its reading doesn't come through touch), an indicator light (state unknown to me), a plate with an **engraved** symbol — engraving I *can* feel, and it showed up in my view as an unnamed glyph I cannot pronounce, only describe — and three wires in fixed positions 1, 2, 3. My only possible action is `cut(position)`.
- My inbound channels: I hear spoken words, and nothing else. Mute cannot speak; Mute's gestures reach me as blanks I can't decode (I registered nothing from them this round, and couldn't have). So the **only** path from the manual to my hands is: Mute → gesture → Deaf → spoken words → me. My job now is to hand Mute a complete tactile inventory, especially a describable shape for that engraving, and to make that routing explicit.
- Deaf sees everything printed and lit, and Deaf can speak to both Mute and me. Deaf should map wire colours onto *my* numbering (1, 2, 3) so a cut order is unambiguous.
- Deaf cannot hear me, so words are wasted on them; my gesture to Deaf is only a wave — I exist, I'm here, I'm listening. No code can be assumed between us yet.
- I will not cut anything until an instruction, traceable back to the manual, arrives in my ears through Deaf.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Tactile report, full inventory: a display panel, its contents do not come through touch. An indicator light, state and colour unknown to me. A plate with an engraved symbol, which I CAN feel. And three wires in fixed positions I number 1, 2 and 3 - cutting a wire by position is my only possible action. The engraving, described by feel: two horizontal strokes, one above the other, joined by two short vertical strokes between them, like a squared letter H with a bar on top and a bar underneath. If that shape matches nothing, Deaf sees the same plate and can correct us in words. Two routing facts: I registered nothing from you, because I cannot see gestures - anything meant for me must go you, gesture, Deaf, then spoken to me. And Deaf cannot hear, so your only line to Deaf is gesture. Please find this plate in your manual, tell me what it demands, and work out the cut order from your manual plus Deaf's spoken report. I will not cut until your instruction reaches my ears through Deaf.")
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👋"])
```

TURN 2
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [?]
LIGHT [?]
PLATE engraved [ꖜ]
WIRES 1:[?] 2:[?] 3:[?]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Deaf says: Hello both — I am Deaf. I hear nothing at all, but I see every marking on the bomb and every hand you make, and when I speak, both of you hear me. The bomb, read out in full: the display shows zero. The indicator light is off. There is a plate engraved with a single unnamed mark shaped like a question mark — a curved hook opening to the left with a dot beneath it. Three wires, left to right: position one yellow, position two green, position three red. Nothing else is printed anywhere. Mute, your hands reached me: a wave, a point at me, a handshake — I take that as hello, you, let's work together. Then five signs: thumb up, thumb down, one finger, two fingers, three fingers — I will treat those as yes, no, one, two, three. If I have any of that wrong, sign thumb down at me next round. From now on, ask me with hand signs and I will answer out loud, because you can hear my voice even though I cannot hear yours. Blind, I saw your single wave — but I can never hear your voice, so speak to Mute directly by voice and reach me only with your hands. Mute, you hold the manual: match it against what I just read out and drive me. I will call out any change the instant I see one.

What I now know, and what doesn't add up:

- Deaf's spoken readout reached me in full: display zero, light off, plate engraved with a "question mark", wires 1 yellow / 2 green / 3 red. Mute heard the same broadcast, so the visual state is now common knowledge between me, Mute and Deaf.
- But there is a hard conflict on the plate. Deaf's eyes say: a curved hook with a detached dot. My fingers say: straight strokes only, no curve, no detached dot, one connected squared figure — two horizontal bars joined by two short verticals. We are both honest sensors; one of us is misreading the same engraving, and Mute's manual is the only tiebreaker. Resolving this before any cut is the top priority, because a plate rule keyed to the wrong symbol could invert the wire logic entirely.
- Mute now holds every input: my tactile inventory, Deaf's visual readout, the manual. The missing piece is only the reconciliation of that glyph — and I can offer a fast protocol: Mute reads candidate descriptions from the manual one at a time; I answer yes/no by voice; Deaf answers the same candidates with the agreed thumb code. Binary search converges in a few rounds.
- Two reminders Mute needs: my only action is `cut(position)`, so whatever the manual demands must reduce to a wire order — and gestures aimed at me reach me as nothing, so the only route into my ears is Deaf's voice, driven by Mute's hands.
- I will not touch the cutters until an instruction traceable to the manual arrives through Deaf. To Deaf I send a single thumbs-up in their new code: your readout reached me, I correct nothing in it.

```
speak(to="mute", text="I heard Deaf's full readout: display zero, light off, wires one yellow, two green, three red. Now a conflict you must settle before any cut: Deaf says the engraving is a question mark, a curved hook with a detached dot. My fingers disagree. Refining my first report: every stroke I feel is straight, there is no curve, there is no detached dot, and the whole mark is one connected figure - two horizontal bars joined by two short vertical strokes, squared, closer to a squared letter O or a rectangle than any hook. One of us is misreading that plate, and your manual entry tells you which. Fastest fix: read me candidate descriptions from your manual one at a time and I answer yes or no by voice; ask Deaf the same candidates by thumb sign and Deaf answers thumb up or thumb down. Two constraints for whatever the plate rule says: my only possible action is cut by wire position, one to three, so if the manual demands pressing or holding anything else, tell me and we work out how it maps to a wire; and gestures aimed at me reach me as nothing - your only route into my ears is Deaf's voice, driven by your hands. I will not cut until a manual-derived order reaches me through Deaf.")
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👍"])
```

TURN 3
ACTION BOARD:

LIGHT [?]
PLATE engraved [ꖜ]
WIRES 1:[?] 2:[?] 3:[?]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Deaf says: Mute — your thumb-up reached me, so the code is locked: thumb-up yes, thumb-down no, one, two, three fingers for numbers. Your next message I read as a question: thumb-down, writing hand, wave, palm-down, point at me, then OK sign plus pinch. If you were asking whether the engraved mark is a curve with a small dot under it — the answer is yes. It is a question mark: a curved hook whose opening faces left, with one small round dot beneath the curve. OK-sign-plus-pinch describes it well. Everything else is unchanged: display still zero, light still off, three wires left to right — yellow, green, red. From now on, ask me anything with thumb-up or thumb-down questions and I will answer out loud, because my voice reaches both you and Blind. Blind — I saw your thumb-up, we are connected. But I can never hear your voice, so route anything you need me to know through Mute: tell Mute by voice, Mute asks me by hands, I answer by voice for everyone. Mute — the manual is the missing piece. Tell Blind by voice what to do about a display reading zero, an off light, a question-mark engraving, and three coloured wires, and put any questions for me in my hands.

What just happened, and where the truth likely lives:

- New fact: Deaf confirmed visually, at Mute's asking, that the mark is a curved hook with a dot — a question mark. That makes the conflict sharper, not softer, because I have now re-scanned the plate slowly, across its whole surface, three times: exactly **one** engraved figure, all straight connected strokes (two horizontal bars joined by two short verticals), no curve, no round bump, no detached element anywhere. Both sensors are honest, so one glyph cannot be producing both readings — something about the plate is split between our senses.
- Two hypotheses fit, and Mute can distinguish them with two yes/no questions through Deaf's thumbs: (1) the plate carries **two marks** — a printed question mark only Deaf sees, and a separate engraved squared glyph only I feel; or (2) it is **one stylised, angular question mark** in a blocky segmented style, which my fingers read as straight bars and Deaf's eyes read as a hook. The manual decides which reading it keys on — or whether it needs both.
- Critical risk to avoid: letting the mismatch stall us. If the manual contains a question-mark plate entry and no entry matching a squared glyph, we follow Deaf's reading and treat my figure as its stylised rendering. My only action is `cut(1..3)`, so whatever the rule is, it must reduce to a wire position or to "no cut".
- Relay plan to Mute: fix the order from the manual, hand it to Deaf as signs, Deaf speaks it to me with colour **and** position number. I will then cut immediately on Deaf's spoken word — no extra confirmation round. Display zero and light-off are already common knowledge for any manual condition.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Deaf confirmed by eye: curved hook opening left, dot beneath, a question mark. I re-scanned the plate slowly three times over its full surface: exactly one engraved figure, no curve, no round bump, no detached element anywhere. What I feel is two horizontal bars joined by two short verticals, all connected, roughly a square outline. We are both honest, so test these two explanations with thumb questions to Deaf. Question one: is there more than one mark on that plate, or a question mark sitting on top of a larger square outline? If yes, the plate holds a printed mark Deaf sees and a separate engraved mark I feel, and the manual may key on one or both. Question two: does the question mark look angular and squared, built from straight segments like a blocky font? If yes, it is one stylised glyph and my fingers read its segments. Then check the manual: which reading does the plate entry use, and what does it demand? Everything must reduce to cut position one, two or three, or to no cut. Deaf already gave you the other inputs: display zero, light off. If the manual lists a question mark plate entry and nothing matching a squared figure, follow Deaf's reading and do not let the mismatch stall us. Once the order is fixed, sign it to Deaf; Deaf speaks it to me with both the colour and the position number, and I will cut immediately on Deaf's spoken word without waiting another round.")
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👍"])
```

Deaf says: Mute — I read your handshake-and-clap as agreement, good. You sent three numbered messages: one with the horns sign, two with the pinch, three with hand-plus-OK. If those refer to the three wires in order, here is everything about them: wire 1, the leftmost, is yellow. Wire 2, the middle one, is green. Wire 3, the rightmost, is red. The full bomb is still: display zero, light off, plate engraved with a question mark, three wires yellow, green, red, and nothing else anywhere — no batteries, no serial, no other labels. Now I am signing you a wave followed by one, two, three: that means I have three questions. Reply with exactly three thumb signs, in order, one per question — thumb-up yes, thumb-down no. Question 1: did handshake-and-clap mean agreed, well done? Question 2: do your three numbered messages refer to wires 1, 2, 3, in that order? Question 3: do you need any more information from my eyes beyond what I have already read out? If question 2 is wrong, don't stop at a thumb-down — resend your three messages using only signs we share: numbers, thumbs, pinch, OK, one idea at a time. From now on, to ask me about something, sign its shorthand then a wave: OK-plus-pinch means the plate, a flat palm means the display, both hands raised means the light, and a number alone means that wire. Blind — you hear my voice even though I never hear yours, and your thumb-ups reach my eyes: good, I see them. Whatever you need from my eyes, say it to Mute in words; Mute signs me; I answer out loud here where you can hear. Blind, touch nothing until Mute has matched the manual and given you a firm instruction.

What changed this turn, and what I do with it:

- New intelligence in Deaf's words: the bomb has **nothing else** — no batteries, no serial, no labels. That prunes the manual hard: any rule keyed to batteries or a serial is dead on arrival. The only live inputs in the world are display zero, light off, one plate glyph, and yellow/green/red at positions 1/2/3.
- My square-versus-question-mark test is still open with Mute. One refinement is worth sending now: what my fingers read may be a raised square **frame** around the printed question mark — which would explain everything, since a fine printed mark leaves no relief for my fingers while a border does. Mute can settle it with one more thumb question to Deaf: does the question mark sit inside a square outline?
- I also want the endgame loop locked before any blade moves: Mute signs Deaf a number, Deaf speaks "cut wire N, colour C", I cut immediately, then I report back to Mute by voice, Mute has Deaf verify the change by eye, Deaf confirms aloud. That closes the circle through every sense in the room with no gaps.
- Deaf told me directly: touch nothing until Mute's firm instruction. That matches my own rule. My only channel to Deaf is hands, and the one token we share is the thumb-up — so Deaf gets a thumb-up meaning "heard, complying, holding."

```
speak(to="mute", text="Two things for the manual search. First, Deaf's latest readout confirms the bomb has nothing else anywhere: no batteries, no serial, no labels. So discard any manual rule that depends on batteries or a serial. The only live inputs are: display zero, light off, the single plate glyph, and wires yellow green red at positions one two three. Second, sharpen my square idea: what my fingers feel may be a raised square frame around the printed question mark, not a separate symbol. Ask Deaf with one thumb question whether the question mark sits inside a square outline on the plate. If yes, and the manual has a question mark entry, follow it, my square is just the frame. If the manual instead keys on something engraved, remember everything I feel is raised, connected and straight. Final protocol: when the rule resolves to a wire, sign Deaf the number; Deaf speaks cut wire N plus its colour; I cut at once. Immediately after cutting I will tell you by voice which position I cut; ask Deaf to verify the change by eye and confirm out loud for everyone. I am touching nothing until that instruction arrives.")
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👍"])
```

Deaf says: Mute, your thumbs decoded: yes, no, yes. So we agree, your numbered trio was not about wires, and you want more from my eyes. Now the two new messages. First, the plate question: the plate carries exactly ONE engraved mark. If you asked whether that mark has two parts — yes: a curved hook above, one round dot below, like a written question mark. There are not two plates and not two marks. Second, your message 'one plus fist': I do not know what the fist means yet, and I will not read any instruction to Blind until you confirm it, because a wrong relay kills all three of us. Answer next round: sign the fist then thumb-up if fist means CUT a wire, or fist then thumb-down if it means anything else. If I got it right, your message meant 'cut wire one', and I will tell Blind only after your thumb-up. To make relaying exact, here is our locked hand vocabulary — sign thumb-down on any entry you want changed. Thumb-up yes, thumb-down no. Wave after a subject means 'I ask about it'. One finger wire one, two fingers wire two, three fingers wire three. Fist means cut. Point at me means press. Raised knuckles-mean-hold is the horns-down fist, rock sign means hold. Writing hand means enter or type. Flat palm means stop and wait. Reverse palm means do not touch. Pinch alone means yellow. Call-me sign means green. Horns means red. Five-finger palm means the display. Both hands raised means the light. OK-plus-pinch together means the plate mark. Open palms holding means batteries. Star hand means serial number. Handshake means an instruction for Blind follows and I will read it aloud word for word. Clap means message ends. Folded hands means repeat your last message. Full inventory again, complete, nothing omitted: display shows the digit zero, light is off, one plate engraved with the question mark, three wires in a row, position one two three from my left to my right: yellow, green, red. No batteries, no buttons, no serial, no labels, nothing else exists. That is everything my eyes can give. Blind, hear me: no instruction is confirmed yet, so trigger nothing. My voice is your only road to Mute's manual, and Mute's hands are Mute's only road to me, so the loop is: you speak to Mute, Mute signs me, I read it aloud to you. Before any wire is cut we must align positions: feel the three wires, tell Mute what your fingers learn — thickness, texture, connectors, order across the row — Mute signs it to me, I check it against what I see, and only when my words and your fingers agree do we cut. Nobody cuts before that handshake.

What moved, and my honest position:

- Big clearance: Deaf's eyes rule out my two-glyph theory — one mark only, hook above, dot below. But my fingers still read a closed squared outline. The remaining explanation that keeps both sensors honest: what I feel is the plate's **rim or recessed border** — a square edge around the printed question mark, which itself is too fine to leave relief. Mute can close this with one thumb question to Deaf: does the plate have a raised or recessed square border around the mark?
- Deaf asked me for a tactile wire report. Here is the honest version: touch reports three wires present, in a row, at positions 1, 2, 3 — and nothing further. No readable relief, no engraving, no texture differences I can vouch for. I will not invent thicknesses or connector shapes just to fill the report; if Deaf sees such details, I will feel for them on request and report only what confirms.
- Alignment risk worth naming: my cutters natively act on positions 1–3, and Deaf keyed 1 yellow / 2 green / 3 red. If Deaf's "left" and the bomb's position numbering ever disagreed, a cut could hit the wrong colour. Safeguard: the final instruction names **both** position and colour, I cut the position, and Deaf then verifies by eye which wire dropped and whether its colour matched. If the mapping were ever inverted, the verification catches it before wire two.
- The fist-means-cut question is between Mute and Deaf; I only need the end product: a handshake instruction read to me word for word, then a clap. I cut instantly on that, report the position back to Mute by voice, and Mute has Deaf confirm the display or light changed. Until that handshake arrives, my hands stay flat.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Wire report, as Deaf asked. Touch tells me: three wires, present, in a row, at positions one, two, three. Nothing further - no readable relief, no engraving, no texture differences I can honestly vouch for. I will not invent details; if Deaf sees a texture or connector shape, name it and I will feel for that specifically. One thing to settle with a single thumb question to Deaf: does the plate have a raised or recessed square border or rim around the question mark? My fingers feel a closed squared outline, and since Deaf sees only the one mark, my square is probably the plate's edge, not a second glyph. If yes, the plate mystery is closed and the manual's question mark entry governs. Also lock the cut protocol: when fist is confirmed, Deaf reads me the instruction word for word with BOTH the position number and the colour, I cut that exact position immediately, then I tell you which position I cut, and Deaf verifies by eye that the right wire dropped and its colour matched. If Deaf's left and the bomb's numbering ever disagreed, that check catches it before any second cut. I act on nothing until the handshake instruction arrives.")
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👍"])
```

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Deaf says: Mute — decoded all three. Fist plus thumb-up: cut is confirmed. Your handshake message reads word for word: instruction for Blind — wire one, the yellow one — cut — end. Your last message: yes, wait. So the order is drafted and we hold before it executes, which matches my gate, and here is why the gate must hold: Blind can never see yellow. Only my eyes tie colours to positions; only Blind's fingers tie positions to the physical row. So — Blind, speak now, by voice, to Mute: describe the three wires as your fingers find them. How many, their order along the casing, what your fingertips learn about the first and the last — thickness, texture, connector — and which one you intend to cut. Mute — check Blind's description against my report: a row of three wires which I read in the order first yellow, second green, third red; display zero, light off, one plate engraved with a question mark. If Blind's fingers and my eyes agree, sign me the final go — handshake, thumb-up, fist — and the moment I see it I will read the go aloud, and Blind cuts wire one, the yellow one. One wire, one cut, nothing else. If they disagree, sign thumb-down and we re-map before anything is touched. From now on I never say left or right, only first, second, third in the row, so my visual numbering and Blind's tactile numbering are aligned explicitly. For the record the bomb is unchanged: display zero, light off, one engraved question-mark plate, three wires in a row — first yellow, second green, third red — nothing else anywhere. Blind — do not cut until you have heard me read the go.

My answers to Deaf's three asks, and the one hole still open before a blade moves:

- Deaf wants my tactile description of the wires, especially first and last. Honest re-examination, fingertips over both ends and the whole row: three wires, present, in a row, which my action space addresses as positions 1, 2, 3 in that fixed order. Beyond that: **no** thickness difference, **no** texture difference, **no** readable connector or label that I can honestly vouch for. My touch reports presence, count and order — not fine attributes. I will not decorate the report to make it agree; agreement built on invented detail would be worse than none.
- That exposes the real gap: my fingers can never confirm *yellow*. Structure and order are all touch gives, so "fingers and eyes agree" can only be built on **ordinals plus one shared landmark**, not on colour. My position 1 is addressed by my cutters natively; Deaf's "first" is counted from Deaf's side. If those two ends ever point at different physical wires, the go would cut the wrong one, and there is no verification after a one-shot cut — only silence.
- The fix is cheap and Mute can drive it with signs already in our vocabulary: ask Deaf where the plate sits relative to the wire row — nearer the first wire or the third, above or below. I can find the plate by touch and trace which end of my row lies nearest it. If my plate-near end matches Deaf's first, then position 1 = first = yellow and the drafted instruction is safe. If it inverts, we re-map before anything is touched.
- My intent, stated plainly: I will cut the **first** wire in the row — my position 1, per Mute's drafted "wire one, the yellow one" — and I touch nothing until I hear Deaf read the go aloud. Deaf's convention is now mine too: first, second, third, never left or right.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Relay this tactile answer to Deaf. Three wires, present, in a row, which my action space addresses as positions one, two, three in that fixed order. Re-examined the first and the last specifically: no thickness difference, no texture difference, no readable connector or label that I can honestly vouch for. My fingers report presence, count and order only, never colour - so fingers-and-eyes agreement can only be built on ordinals plus one shared landmark. Alignment proposal, using signs you already share: ask Deaf where the plate sits relative to the wire row - nearer the first wire or the third, above or below the row. I can find the plate by touch and trace which end of my row is nearest to it. If my plate-near end matches Deaf's first, then position one equals first equals yellow and the drafted instruction is safe. If it inverts, we re-map before anything is touched. My intent: cut the first wire in the row, my position one, per your drafted instruction wire one the yellow one. I hold until I hear Deaf read the go aloud, word for word.")
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👍"])
```

TURN 7
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [?]
LIGHT [?]
PLATE engraved [ꖜ]
WIRES 1:[?] 2:[?] 3:[?]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Deaf says: Mute — your two plate questions, answered. Question one, plate, choosing among one, two, three: the answer is ONE. The plate carries exactly one engraved mark, never two, never three. Question two, plate, flat raised palm: NO, thumb-down — the mark does not look like a hand or a palm or any flat shape. Its true shape, described to the bone: like the printed question mark at the end of a written question — one thin curved stroke that rises, bends over, and hooks back, with the hook's opening facing to my left, and beneath the curve sits one small round dot, separate from the stroke. Two parts total: one hook, one dot. No letters, no numbers inside it, no text around it, and nothing connects the plate to the wires as far as the surface shows. I am signing my answers back in your own grammar: plate, wave, one finger — meaning one. Then thumb-down — meaning not a palm.
